claims.text: Atomic size mismatch causes lattice distortion in multi-component concentrated alloys.
The extent of lattice distortion governs alloy strength.
The extent of lattice distortion governs deformation behavior.
Lattice distortion strengthens these alloys by impeding dislocation motion.
Systematic changes in alloy composition and heat treatment can modulate lattice distortion.
Increasing lattice distortion raises the energy barriers for dislocation movement.
Higher barriers to dislocation movement lead to higher yield strength.
Increased lattice distortion may shift deformation toward more brittle failure.
Alloys with higher measured lattice distortion are predicted to have greater yield strength than baseline alloys processed to minimize distortion.
Alloys with higher measured lattice distortion are predicted to exhibit altered, possibly more brittle, deformation modes relative to the baseline.
Alloys processed to minimize lattice distortion have lower yield strength.
Alloys processed to minimize lattice distortion exhibit conventional ductile deformation.
The proposed relationship should hold when atomic size mismatch dominates the microstructure.
Precipitation or ordering may overshadow the effects of lattice distortion.
X-ray diffraction can be used to quantify lattice distortion in the proposed comparison.
TEM can be used to analyze dislocation density in the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The intervention changes both composition and heat treatment while the conditions assert that lattice distortion is the only significant variable. Composition and heat treatment can independently alter phase constitution, ordering, precipitation, grain structure, and dislocation state, so the proposed design does not by itself isolate lattice distortion.
